title: The data-science lifecycle
kicker: ENCT 202 · Foundation of Data Science · Chapter 1
subtitle: Data science is a loop, not a line: ask, collect, clean, explore, model, check, deploy — and go round again.

sections.title: What data science is
sections.body: Data science extracts knowledge and decisions from data using statistics, programming and domain understanding. It sits between three skills: mathematics/statistics (what is true?), computing (how to do it at scale?) and the domain (is it meaningful?). Related terms: analytics describes the past, machine learning learns patterns to predict, big data means volume, velocity and variety beyond one machine.

questions.prompt: Which best states the aim of data science?

choices.text: Turn data into decisions using statistics, computing and domain knowledge.
Store as much data as possible.

sections.title: The lifecycle
sections.body: Typical stages (CRISP-DM style): business understanding → data collection → preparation → exploration → modeling → evaluation → deployment → monitoring. Results at any stage often send you back: poor evaluation means revisit features or collect more data.

questions.prompt: Poor evaluation results usually send you…

choices.text: Back to earlier stages (cleaning, features, more data).

figures.caption: Figure 1.2.1 — lifecycle
figures.note: Follow the arrows; the “not yet” arrow is the loop.
figures.script:
diagram("Question -> Collect : what data answers it?
Collect -> Clean : raw data
Clean -> Explore : tidy data
Explore -> Model : features
Model -> Evaluate : predictions
Evaluate -> Deploy : good enough
Evaluate -> Clean : not yet
Deploy -> Question : monitor and refine");

Variables are numeric (discrete or continuous) or categorical (nominal, or ordinal if ordered). The type decides which summary and chart are allowed.

sections.title: Sources and tools
sections.body: Sources: databases, APIs, sensors/IoT, web scraping, surveys, logs. Typical tools: Python (pandas, NumPy, scikit-learn), SQL, notebooks, visualisation libraries. Data engineers build pipelines; analysts explain; scientists model.

responses.title: Correct.
responses.body: Volume and velocity are big-data traits.

sections.title: Good questions and samples
sections.body: A vague goal (“improve sales”) becomes a measurable question (“which customers will churn in 30 days?”). Sampling matters: a random sample represents the population; convenience or self-selected samples are biased. More data does not fix a biased sample.

worked.why: A shop has 400 customers; 60 churned last month. Churn rate:
Predicting “no churn” for everyone is right 85 % of the time yet useless — accuracy alone misleads on imbalanced data.

questions.prompt: An online poll answered only by people who chose to click is…

sections.title: What data cannot tell you
sections.body: Correlation is not causation; past patterns may not hold; a model is only as good as its data (“garbage in, garbage out”). Randomised experiments (A/B tests) are how causal claims are earned.
